title: Accelerated and Stable Convergence with Anchored Generalized Optimistic Method
one_liner: An update rule for min-max and related equilibrium problems that combines optimism with anchoring to get fast last-iterate convergence using one or two operator calls.
lead: Many machine learning problems are not plain minimization. In min-max games and monotone variational inequalities, the update must settle to a balance point where no local move can improve one side without worsening another, because the two sides are pushing against each other at the same time. Simple gradient descent (repeatedly moving in the direction that most reduces the current objective) can cycle around that point. Extragradient fixes some of the cycling but usually needs two operator evaluations per step. GOMA adds an anchor term to optimistic updates and gets stronger last-iterate guarantees because the optimistic part offsets rotational drift while the anchor keeps the trajectory from wandering, in both deterministic and random (noise-driven) settings.

problem.h2: Equilibrium problems can rotate instead of settling
paras: In a min-max problem, one variable is trying to decrease an objective while another is trying to increase it. The resulting update field is often rotational. Move one variable a little and the best response of the other variable changes direction. Basic first-order methods can therefore keep orbiting the solution instead of approaching it step by step.

Extragradient uses a lookahead correction to reduce that orbiting, but it usually needs two operator evaluations each iteration. That extra cost matters in online and random settings, where each evaluation can be noisy or expensive. The challenge is to retain stability while also getting fast convergence of the actual iterate you keep at the end of training.

callout.html: The algorithm must cancel rotational drift without paying too much per step, and it must make the last iterate itself converge rather than only an average of iterates.

steps.text: Maintain the point whose equilibrium error you ultimately care about.
Use recent operator information to counter predictable rotational motion.
Pull the update toward a reference point with a carefully scheduled weight.

steps.b: Tune step sizes on two time scales

Prove that the actual final iterate reaches a small operator norm, not only an average iterate.

paras: The paper changes the update rule used for monotone equilibrium problems. It takes a generalized optimistic method and adds anchoring inspired by Halpern iteration, which is a fixed-point method that repeatedly mixes the current iterate with a reference point. The added anchor introduces a stabilizing pull while the optimistic part handles the rotational structure of the operator field.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: last-iterate equilibrium error
hidden.name: last-iterate equilibrium error
paras: The paper measures progress with the squared norm of the operator at the current iterate. In plain terms, the operator is the update field produced by the equilibrium problem. If that field is large, the current point is still far from balance because the problem is still pushing strongly in some direction. If that field is near zero, the point is close to equilibrium.

This choice matters because many older guarantees focus on averages of iterates. Averages can hide oscillation: the average may look good even while the actual current point is still cycling. A last-iterate guarantee is stronger for practice because the algorithm returns one final point, not an average of every point it ever visited.

heat.caption: Darker cells indicate states where the current iterate is genuinely close to equilibrium.

reads.html: The quantity asks whether the final point the algorithm keeps is still being pushed around by the game.
A small squared operator norm at the last iterate means the method has nearly reached a zero of the monotone operator.

paras: Optimistic methods are useful in games because the update field often has short-term predictability. If the operator tends to rotate in a regular way, the previous operator value contains information about where the next push will point. Using that information cancels part of the rotational drift.

Anchoring adds a different effect. It keeps each iterate tied to a reference point through a scheduled mixture. This matters because optimism alone can still drift or amplify noise when the operator is random. The anchor supplies a stabilizing bias that shrinks over time, so early steps stay controlled while later steps can still approach the true solution.

The two-time-scale design is what lets the method claim both acceleration and stability. One schedule governs how aggressively the method follows the optimistic correction. Another governs how quickly the anchor weight fades. In the deterministic setting, this balance yields the stated fast decrease of last-iterate squared operator norm. In the random setting, the single-call form still converges under unbounded variance because the anchor prevents noise from causing unrestricted wandering.

stages.s: Current iterate and recent operator values
Predict rotational drift with an optimistic correction
Pull the iterate toward the anchor point
Combine both effects with scheduled step sizes
Update the current iterate and repeat
Final iterate with reduced operator norm

math.h2: The equation: optimistic step plus anchor mixture
math.words: Update the current point using an optimistic operator correction and a shrinking pull toward a fixed anchor point.
math.equation: new_point = anchor_weight * anchor_point + remaining_weight * optimistic_update(current_point, previous_operator_value)
symbols: the next iterate produced by the method
the amount of pull toward the anchor on this step
the fixed reference point used to stabilize the iteration
the part of the step assigned to the optimistic update
the correction that uses recent operator information to reduce rotational drift

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the current game update keeps turning the iterate clockwise around the solution.
The optimistic term uses the previous turn direction to offset part of the next clockwise push.
At the same time, a small anchor weight keeps the iterate from flying outward when the correction is noisy.
As the anchor weight shrinks, the method relies more on the corrected dynamics and less on the fixed reference point.

math.note: The exact paper method contains several related variants, but they all share the same structural idea: prediction for the rotation and anchoring for stability.

bars.h2: What the result should look like

charts.title: Plain or weakly corrected updates
charts.note: Cheap updates alone are not enough because the iterate can keep circling the equilibrium.

charts.title: Anchored generalized optimism
charts.note: The method pays a modest algorithmic cost for a stronger current-iterate guarantee because the anchor controls drift while optimism cancels rotation.

items.html: If the anchor keeps too much weight for too long, the method can stay biased toward the reference point and approach the true equilibrium more slowly.
If the stabilizing pull disappears before the optimistic term has enough reliable signal, noisy or rotational problems can destabilize the trajectory again.
The guarantees rely on monotonicity and Lipschitz continuity, which means the operator behaves in a controlled way. Outside that setting, the same schedule may not produce the claimed rates.
The method is strongest when the operator field is monotone, the schedules for optimism and anchoring are matched to the theory, and the application needs the last iterate itself to be reliable.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a two-dimensional bilinear min-max game, which is a standard rotating test case. Run basic gradient descent, an extragradient baseline, and an anchored optimistic method. Track the current iterate and the norm of the game operator at every step.

The important plot is not only the path of the iterates but also the final-iterate residual over time. The anchored optimistic method should approach the center more directly and keep the residual decreasing, while the plain method circles. Then add random noise to the operator call and compare the single-call anchored variant against a single-call baseline without anchoring.
demo.closing: A convincing demo shows that the kept iterate is better because optimism predicts the rotational drift and anchoring stops noise from turning that correction into instability.
